name: Kichwa
region: Ecuador, southern Colombia (Inga) and the Peruvian Amazon (Chachapoyas, Lamas)
defining_innovation: Torero's Quechua II-B, the northern Quechua of Ecuador, Colombia and the Amazon, simplified in grammar and much shaped by Spanish contact.

chapters.title: Northern Quechua
chapters.body:
Kichwa, the Ecuadorian form of the name, is spoken by several hundred thousand people in the Ecuadorian highlands and Amazon, and related varieties reach into Colombia (Inga) and the Peruvian lowlands. Its presence in Ecuador is usually traced to the Inca conquest in the late 15th century and to its spread as a colonial *lengua general*, though some scholars argue for earlier trade contacts. Compared with southern Quechua it has lost the possessive person suffixes on nouns and simplified its verb agreement.

In the town of Salcedo, Kichwa grammar combined with almost entirely Spanish vocabulary to create *Media Lengua*, one of the clearest examples of a mixed language anywhere.

chapters.title: Sounds and a Unified Spelling
chapters.body:
Kichwa sounds noticeably different from the Quechua of Peru and Bolivia. It has no uvular `q`: the old sound merged with plain *k*, so the word for 'lake' is *kucha* where Cusco has *qucha*. It keeps the sound *sh* that Southern Quechua lost, as in *shimi* 'mouth, language'. In many highland dialects, such as that of Imbabura, stops become voiced after a nasal, so that suffixes beginning with *k* or *t* can be pronounced *g* or *d*. It also lacks the aspirated and ejective consonants of Cusco and Bolivia.

These differences, and the variety among Ecuadorian dialects, made written materials hard to share. From the 1980s Indigenous organisations and the national bilingual education system promoted a unified written standard, *Kichwa Unificado*, with a single spelling for all dialects. The name itself reflects that choice: the Spanish-based spelling *Quichua* gave way to *Kichwa*, with *k* and *w*. The standard is used in schools, official documents and media. Some speakers feel it favours no one's actual speech, and in practice local pronunciation varies widely beneath the shared spelling.

speakers.note: Ecuador's 2010 census counted 591,448 Kichwa speakers; smaller varieties in Colombia and the Peruvian Amazon are more endangered.

turning_points.title: North with the Inca
turning_points.description: Quechua spreads into Ecuador with Inca conquest and then with Spanish missionaries, replacing many local languages. How much of the spread is Inca and how much colonial, and whether Quechua arrived earlier through trade, is debated.

sources.citation: Adelaar, Willem F. H. with Pieter C. Muysken. 2004. The Languages of the Andes. Cambridge: Cambridge University Press.

turning_points.title: Media Lengua
turning_points.description: Kichwa speakers in the Salcedo area develop Media Lengua, a mixed language with Kichwa grammar and suffixes attached to nearly all Spanish word stems.

sources.citation: Muysken, Pieter. 1997. Media Lengua. In Contact Languages: A Wider Perspective, ed. Sarah G. Thomason. Amsterdam: John Benjamins.

turning_points.title: Ecuador's constitution
turning_points.description: Ecuador's 2008 constitution makes Kichwa and Shuar official languages of intercultural relations, alongside Spanish, following decades of intercultural bilingual education.

sources.citation: Constitución de la República del Ecuador. 2008. Artículo 2.
